Water-soluble vs. fat-soluble vitamins: which are which, and how does storage differ?

Water-soluble: the B vitamins and vitamin C; most are not stored in large amounts and excess is excreted in urine. Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K; stored in liver and adipose tissue, so they can accumulate to toxic levels.
Thiamine (B1): coenzyme form and main role?
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP). It is needed to decarboxylate α-keto acids, e.g., by pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (and by transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway).
FAD and FMN. They carry electrons in redox reactions, e.g., FAD in succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) and FMN in Complex I.
NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, which carry a hydride (2 electrons + H⁺). NAD⁺ mostly accepts electrons in catabolism; NADPH mostly donates them in biosynthesis and antioxidant defense.
Pantothenic acid (B5): what coenzyme does it form?
Coenzyme A (CoA), which carries acyl groups (e.g., acetyl-CoA) through a high-energy thioester bond.
Pyridoxine (B6): coenzyme form and main roles?

Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). It is needed for amino acid metabolism: transamination (aminotransferases) and amino acid decarboxylation (e.g., making neurotransmitters). It is also a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase.
Folate (B9): coenzyme form and why is it essential for dividing cells?
Tetrahydrofolate (THF) carries one-carbon units needed to make purines and thymidylate (dTMP). Deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic anemia and, in pregnancy, neural tube defects.
Vitamin C: biochemical role and deficiency?
It is a reducing cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in collagen synthesis, and it is also an antioxidant. Deficiency (scurvy) weakens collagen, causing bleeding gums and poor wound healing.
Which five coenzymes does the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex require?
TPP (from B1), lipoic acid, coenzyme A (B5), FAD (B2), and NAD⁺ (B3).
Why can thiamine deficiency raise blood lactate?
Without TPP, pyruvate dehydrogenase can't turn pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. Pyruvate builds up and is converted to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺.
What is a protein's solvation layer (hydration shell)?
The layer of water molecules organized around a dissolved protein's surface, hydrogen-bonding with polar and charged groups.
How do interactions between water and nonpolar side chains contribute to the hydrophobic effect in protein folding?

Burying nonpolar side chains in the protein's core releases the ordered water that surrounded them. This increases the solvent's entropy (ΔS > 0), which makes ΔG of folding more negative. This is the hydrophobic effect, a major driving force of protein folding.
What mainly drives the hydrophobic effect in protein folding?
An entropy increase of the surrounding water. When nonpolar side chains cluster in the core, ordered water is released into the bulk solvent.
Why is a folded protein only marginally more stable than its unfolded form?

Folding lowers the chain's own conformational entropy, which is unfavorable. That cost is offset by the solvent's entropy gain and by favorable enthalpy from H-bonds, van der Waals, and ionic contacts, leaving a net ΔG that is only modestly negative.
How do urea and detergents denature proteins?

Urea disrupts hydrogen bonding and makes it easier for water to solvate nonpolar groups, which weakens the hydrophobic effect. Detergents like SDS coat hydrophobic regions. Both stabilize the unfolded state.
In a transmembrane α-helix, which side chains face the lipid bilayer, and why?
Mostly hydrophobic side chains (e.g., Leu, Ile, Val, Phe). They contact the nonpolar lipid tails, where there is no water to order and no polar partners to satisfy.
Path of electrons from NADH and FADH₂ through the ETC?
NADH → Complex I → ubiquinone (CoQ) → Complex III → cytochrome c → Complex IV → O₂. FADH₂ (from succinate) enters at Complex II → CoQ.
Which ETC complexes pump protons, and why does FADH₂ yield less ATP than NADH?
Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons; Complex II does not. FADH₂ electrons enter at Complex II and bypass Complex I, so fewer protons are pumped (~1.5 ATP per FADH₂ vs. ~2.5 per NADH).
What are the two mobile electron carriers of the ETC?
Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q), a lipid-soluble carrier in the inner membrane, and cytochrome c, a water-soluble heme protein in the intermembrane space.
About how much ATP does complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose yield?
About 30–32 ATP (older textbooks say 36–38). The exact number depends on how cytosolic NADH is shuttled into mitochondria.
What two components make up the proton-motive force?
A chemical gradient (ΔpH: the intermembrane space is more acidic than the matrix) and an electrical gradient (membrane potential: matrix side negative).
Structure and mechanism of ATP synthase?
F₀ is the membrane-embedded proton channel that rotates as H⁺ flows through it. F₁ is the matrix-facing catalytic head, where rotation-driven conformational changes make ATP from ADP + Pᵢ.
How do cyanide and carbon monoxide interfere with aerobic ATP production, and how do their principal mechanisms differ?

Cyanide directly inhibits mitochondrial Complex IV, blocking electron transfer to O₂ and reducing oxidative phosphorylation. Carbon monoxide primarily binds hemoglobin and impairs oxygen delivery; it can also inhibit mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase.
An ATP synthase inhibitor (oligomycin) is added to respiring mitochondria. What happens to O₂ consumption?
It falls. Protons can't flow back through ATP synthase, so the gradient builds until pumping becomes too unfavorable and electron transport slows.
What mainly regulates the rate of oxidative phosphorylation?
ADP (and Pᵢ) availability, known as respiratory control. High ADP speeds ATP synthase, which lowers the gradient and lets electron transport and O₂ use speed up; low ADP slows it.
How are mitochondria involved in apoptosis and oxidative stress?

In the intrinsic pathway, cytochrome c released from the intermembrane space into the cytosol activates caspases. Electron leakage from the ETC also produces reactive oxygen species (e.g., superoxide), which cause oxidative damage.

Why does glucose appear in the urine in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus?

How does the counter-current multiplier build the medullary osmotic gradient?

The thick ascending limb actively pumps NaCl into the interstitium but is impermeable to water. Fluid flowing in opposite directions in the two limbs multiplies this effect into a gradient that rises toward the inner medulla.
How does dehydration change ADH release and urine concentration, and how does this contrast with ADH deficiency or temporary alcohol-induced ADH suppression?

How do the kidneys respond to metabolic acidosis?

Why does blocking lymphatic drainage cause edema?

How does lymph move without a central pump?
Skeletal muscle contraction, breathing-related pressure changes, and smooth muscle in lymphatic walls squeeze it along; one-way valves prevent backflow.

Rationalization: social action increasingly based on efficiency, calculation, and rules rather than tradition or emotion; bureaucracy is its organizational form. The iron cage: people trapped in rule-bound, impersonal systems.

What are the four dimensions of McDonaldization?

Efficiency (the fastest path to a goal), calculability (quantity over quality; what can be counted), predictability (standardized, uniform results), and control (especially by replacing human judgment with nonhuman technology).

Random sampling: how participants are selected from the population; it supports generalizing results (external validity). Random assignment: how participants in the study are placed into conditions; it supports causal conclusions (internal validity).
Why does random assignment allow causal conclusions?
It spreads participant characteristics, both known and unknown possible confounds, roughly evenly across groups, so outcome differences can be attributed to the independent variable.
Volunteers choose either a meditation class or no class; meditators later report less stress. What is the main design flaw?
No random assignment (self-selection). Preexisting differences such as motivation or baseline stress could explain the result, so meditation can't be concluded to cause lower stress.
A trial randomly assigns 200 students from one university to a drug or placebo. What does this design support, and what does it not?

It supports a causal conclusion about the drug's effect in this kind of sample (internal validity). It does not ensure the result applies to other populations, such as older adults (limited external validity, because there was no random sampling).
A study comparing groups that were not randomly assigned, often preexisting groups (e.g., two classrooms, smokers vs. nonsmokers). Causal conclusions are weaker than in a true experiment.
A researcher compares pain tolerance across groups defined by recorded biological sex. Why can this comparison alone not establish that sex causes a difference?

Biological sex cannot be randomly assigned as an experimental treatment. Differences between groups may involve confounding factors, measurement choices, and social or physiological influences, so causal attribution requires caution.

The study's purpose, procedures, duration, foreseeable risks and benefits, how confidentiality is protected, and that participation is voluntary, with the right to withdraw at any time without penalty.
What does an institutional review board (IRB) do?

Before human-subjects research starts, it reviews the study to make sure risks are minimized and justified by the benefits, consent procedures are adequate, and participants (especially vulnerable ones) are protected.
What are the three core ethical principles for research with human participants?

Respect for persons (autonomy, informed consent, extra protection for those with diminished autonomy), beneficence (maximize benefits, minimize harm), and justice (fair distribution of research burdens and benefits).
When is deception in research acceptable?
When it is necessary for valid results, risks are minimal, there is no reasonable alternative, an IRB approves it, and participants are debriefed afterward.
Anonymity: even the researchers can't link data to a participant's identity. Confidentiality: researchers can link data to identities but promise not to disclose them.
What extra protections apply to research with children?
Permission from a parent or guardian, plus the child's own assent (agreement) when the child is able to give it. Children, like prisoners, are considered a vulnerable population.
A research participant decides to withdraw. The investigator threatens to withhold compensation already earned unless the participant stays. What is the ethical concern?
Threatening to remove compensation already earned pressures continued participation and undermines voluntary consent and the right to withdraw without inappropriate penalty.
Why is it often unethical to give a placebo to a control group when an effective treatment exists for a serious illness?
Withholding a known effective treatment exposes participants to avoidable harm (beneficence). The new treatment is usually compared with the standard of care instead.

A study finds coffee drinkers have higher lung cancer rates. What is a likely confound?

Internal: how confidently the observed effect can be attributed to the IV (no confounds). External: how well the results generalize to other people, settings, and times.
Reliability vs. validity of a measure?

Reliability: consistency (e.g., test–retest, inter-rater agreement). Validity: whether the measure actually assesses what it is meant to. A measure can be reliable without being valid, but an unreliable measure can't be valid.
What does a double-blind, placebo-controlled design control for?

Placebo effects (expectations of participants who don't know which treatment they received) and experimenter bias (researchers who don't know the group assignments can't influence or interpret outcomes unevenly).
A survey asks students to self-report alcohol use. What bias is likely, and how could it be reduced?
Social desirability bias (under-reporting), plus recall error. Anonymous surveys or objective measures help reduce it.
Which study features strengthen a causal claim rather than just an association?
Random assignment to a manipulated variable, temporality (the cause comes before the effect), control of confounds, and ideally a dose–response relationship and replication.
The typical spread of data around the mean, in the same units as the data. Small SD: values cluster near the mean. Large SD: values are widely spread.
Empirical rule for a normal distribution?
About 68% of values fall within ±1 SD of the mean, about 95% within ±2 SD, and about 99.7% within ±3 SD.
Scores are normally distributed with mean 70 and SD 5. About what percentage scored above 80?

Drugs A and B both lower blood pressure by a mean of 10 mmHg; SD is 2 for A and 8 for B. Interpret.

An extreme outlier is added to a dataset. Which statistics change most?
Mean, SD, and range are sensitive to outliers; median and interquartile range are resistant.
What happens to the mean and SD if you add a constant to every value, or multiply every value by a constant?
Adding a constant c to every value changes the mean to μ + c but leaves SD unchanged. Multiplying every value by c changes the mean to cμ and SD to |c|σ.
Standard deviation vs. standard error of the mean?
SD describes the spread of individual observations. SEM = SD/√n describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean; it shrinks as n grows.
Two group means are plotted with ±1 SD error bars that overlap substantially. What can you conclude?

Not much from the graph alone. Overlapping SD bars mean individual scores overlap a lot between groups, but whether the mean difference is statistically significant requires a statistical test (it also depends on n).
What does a 95% confidence interval for a mean represent?
A range of plausible values for the population mean, calculated by a method that would capture the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples.
Common misreadings of a 95% confidence interval?

It does not mean 95% of individual data points fall inside it, and it does not mean a repeated study's mean will fall inside it 95% of the time. It describes uncertainty about the population parameter.
What makes a confidence interval wider?
More variability (larger SD), a smaller sample, and a higher confidence level (a 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI).
In a randomized, well-controlled trial, the 95% CI for the mean recovery-time difference (drug − placebo) is −4 to −1 days. What does this suggest?

The estimated mean recovery time is 1–4 days shorter with the drug, and the 95% CI excludes 0 (consistent with a two-sided p < 0.05 under corresponding assumptions). Randomization supports—but does not by itself guarantee—a causal interpretation.
The 95% CI for a treatment difference is −2 to +5 units. What can you conclude?
The interval includes 0, so the difference is not statistically significant at α = 0.05. The data fit no effect, but they also fit a moderate benefit or a small harm.
A study reports relative risk = 1.8 (95% CI 0.9–3.6). Interpret.
The interval includes 1 (no difference in risk), so the association is not statistically significant at α = 0.05, even though the point estimate suggests higher risk.

The effect is statistically significant but probably not practically (clinically) meaningful.

1A-018.simple: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the enzyme's active site.
1A-018.why: Because the inhibitor and substrate compete for the same site, adding more substrate can outcompete the inhibitor. More substrate is needed to reach half of V<sub>max</sub>, so the apparent K<sub>m</sub> rises. V<sub>max</sub> is unchanged because at very high substrate concentrations the substrate wins, and the enzyme reaches the same top speed.
1A-018.example: Methotrexate competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, interfering with folate metabolism.
1A-018.mcat: Expect questions on how each inhibitor type changes K<sub>m</sub>, V<sub>max</sub>, and the Michaelis–Menten and Lineweaver–Burk graphs.
1A-018.mistake: Mixing it up with noncompetitive inhibition. Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers V<sub>max</sub> and leaves K<sub>m</sub> unchanged.

4C-030.text:
Faraday's law of induction: a changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an emf, ε = −ΔΦ/Δt; the minus sign reflects Lenz's law (the induced current opposes the change in flux).
Note: Electromagnetic induction is not in the AAMC MCAT content outline, so treat this card as beyond-the-test enrichment. When the MCAT refers to “Faraday's law,” it means Faraday's law of electrolysis (4C, electrolytic cells): the amount of an element deposited (or gas liberated) at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed. Moles of electrons = Q/F = It/F, with F ≈ 96,485 C per mole of electrons; divide by the number of electrons per ion to get moles of element deposited.

1A-041.text:
Simple explanation: How a vitamin dissolves determines how it is absorbed, carried, and stored.
Why it works: Water-soluble vitamins dissolve in plasma and are filtered by the kidneys; fat-soluble vitamins travel with lipids (chylomicrons) and accumulate in tissues.
Common mistake: Treating B12 like other water-soluble vitamins: it is an exception and is stored in the liver for years.

1A-042.text:
Simple explanation: TPP helps remove CO₂ from α-keto acids.
Why it works: Its thiazole ring forms a carbanion that attacks the keto carbon and stabilizes the intermediate left when CO₂ is released.

1A-043.text:
Simple explanation: Flavin coenzymes act as electron carriers in flavoproteins.
Why it works: The flavin ring can accept one or two electrons (with protons), so it can link two-electron donors to one-electron carriers in the ETC.
Common mistake: Thinking FAD floats freely like NAD⁺; it is usually tightly bound as a prosthetic group.

1A-044.text:
Simple explanation: Niacin supplies the nicotinamide ring that carries electrons.
Why it works: Cells keep NAD⁺/NADH mostly oxidized (ready to accept electrons) and NADP⁺/NADPH mostly reduced (ready to donate them).
Common mistake: Mixing up the roles: NADPH, not NADH, drives fatty acid synthesis and keeps glutathione reduced.

1A-045.text:
Simple explanation: CoA is the cell's main carrier of acyl groups.
Why it works: Breaking the thioester releases a lot of free energy, which makes acyl transfers such as citrate synthase's reaction favorable.

1A-046.text:
Simple explanation: PLP handles amino groups.
Why it works: Its aldehyde forms a Schiff base (imine) with an amino acid, which makes the amino group easy to transfer or makes decarboxylation easier.

1A-047.text:
Simple explanation: THF donates single carbons for building nucleotides.
Why it works: Rapidly dividing cells (bone marrow, embryos) need a lot of new DNA, so they are hit first when folate runs low.
Common mistake: Forgetting the drug link: methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, which regenerates THF; that is why it is used against cancer.

1A-048.text:
Simple explanation: Vitamin C keeps the iron in collagen hydroxylases in its active reduced state.
Why it works: Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine stabilize the collagen triple helix through hydrogen bonds and cross-links; without them, connective tissue is weak.

1A-049.text:
Simple explanation: PDH decarboxylates pyruvate, oxidizes the remainder, and attaches it to CoA, so it needs several helpers.
Why it works: TPP decarboxylates; lipoamide carries the acetyl group and electrons; CoA receives the acetyl group; FAD and then NAD⁺ take the electrons.
Common mistake: Leaving out biotin is correct here; biotin belongs to pyruvate carboxylase, not PDH.

1A-050.text:
Simple explanation: A blocked PDH shunts pyruvate toward lactate.
Why it works: Lactate dehydrogenase turns the excess pyruvate into lactate, and less acetyl-CoA reaches the citric acid cycle, so aerobic ATP production falls. Tissues that rely on glucose, such as the brain, are especially affected.

1A-051.text:
Simple explanation: Water molecules arrange themselves around a solute according to how they can interact with it.
Why it works: Polar and charged surface groups form favorable hydrogen bonds and ion–dipole interactions with water, which helps keep the protein dissolved.

1A-052.text: Nonpolar side chains can't form hydrogen bonds with water, so the water next to them has fewer ways to arrange itself. When folding buries these side chains, that constrained water is released into the bulk solvent, increasing its entropy and lowering ΔG (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS). For the MCAT, treat the hydrophobic effect as mainly entropy-driven. Keep in mind that it also has enthalpic contributions that change with temperature and conditions, so don't picture water as forming rigid, identical “cages” around every nonpolar group.

1A-053.text:
Simple explanation: Burying nonpolar groups frees the water that was ordered around them.
Why it works: Less nonpolar surface area means fewer ordered water molecules, so ΔS(solvent) > 0 and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS becomes more negative.
Common mistake: Crediting strong attractions between nonpolar groups; van der Waals contacts help, but the solvent's entropy is the main driver.

1A-054.text:
Simple explanation: Folding balances large opposing terms.
Why it works: Restricting the chain to one shape costs entropy; burying nonpolar groups and forming contacts pays it back, so heat or chemicals can tip the balance.
Common mistake: Assuming folding lowers the total entropy of the system; the solvent gains more entropy than the chain loses.

1A-055.text:
Simple explanation: Denaturants make unfolding less costly.
Why it works: When exposed nonpolar groups are no longer strongly penalized, the folded state loses its advantage and the protein unfolds. Covalent primary structure stays intact.
Common mistake: Thinking denaturants break peptide bonds; they disrupt noncovalent structure (2°, 3°, 4°).

1A-056.text:
Simple explanation: Side chain placement matches the surrounding environment.
Why it works: In water, nonpolar groups are buried to avoid ordering the solvent; in the bilayer, the surroundings are nonpolar, so nonpolar groups face outward and polar groups are hidden or paired.
Common mistake: Applying the soluble-protein rule (hydrophobic inside) to membrane-facing surfaces.

1D-034.text:
Simple explanation: Electrons move to carriers with progressively higher reduction potential.
Why it works: Each transfer is exergonic; the released energy is used by Complexes I, III, and IV to pump protons.

1D-035.text:
Simple explanation: ATP yield follows the number of protons pumped.
Why it works: Skipping Complex I means fewer H⁺ move into the intermembrane space for each pair of electrons, so less ATP synthase turning.

1D-036.text:
Simple explanation: Mobile carriers move electrons between the fixed complexes.
Why it works: CoQ diffuses within the membrane from Complexes I and II to III; cytochrome c moves along the outer face of the inner membrane from III to IV.

1D-037.text:
Simple explanation: Most of the ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation, not glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.
Why it works: 10 NADH × ~2.5 + 2 FADH₂ × ~1.5 + 4 ATP/GTP made directly ≈ 32; the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle delivers cytosolic NADH electrons as FADH₂, giving about 30.
Common mistake: Counting 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH₂; current values are about 2.5 and 1.5.

1D-038.text:
Simple explanation: Protons are pulled back into the matrix both by concentration and by charge.
Why it works: Pumping H⁺ out raises their concentration outside and leaves the matrix negative; both effects favor H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase.

1D-039.text:
Simple explanation: ATP synthase is a rotary motor that couples proton flow to ATP synthesis.
Why it works: Proton flow turns the F₀ rotor and central stalk, which cycles the F₁ catalytic sites through binding ADP + Pᵢ, forming ATP, and releasing it.

1D-040.text: Cyanide binds cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), preventing normal use of oxygen as the final electron acceptor, collapsing electron transport and limiting mitochondrial ATP production. Carbon monoxide poisoning primarily causes tissue hypoxia through high-affinity binding to hemoglobin and impaired oxygen unloading; it may also inhibit mitochondrial Complex IV. Don't assume CO and cyanide act the same way: cyanide's main effect is blocking Complex IV, so cells can't use O₂ even when it is delivered, whereas CO's main effect is reducing O₂ delivery, and the two don't necessarily change cellular O₂ consumption in the same way.

1D-041.text:
Simple explanation: Electron transport and ATP synthesis are coupled through the proton gradient.
Why it works: A gradient that can't be used works like back-pressure on the pumps. An uncoupler does the opposite (see 1D-032): it lets protons leak back, so O₂ use rises while ATP synthesis falls.
Common mistake: Assuming blocking ATP synthase leaves the ETC unaffected.

1D-042.text:
Simple explanation: ATP is made as fast as it is used.
Why it works: Using ATP produces ADP, which feeds ATP synthase; consuming the gradient lets the pumps run faster.

1D-043.text:
Simple explanation: Mitochondria both supply energy and control cell death.
Why it works: Mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization releases cytochrome c; ROS form when electrons reduce O₂ only partway.

3B-044.text: The glomerulus is a tuft of blood capillaries, not a compartment through which filtrate flows. Filtration moves water and small solutes from glomerular blood across the filtration barrier into Bowman’s space. Tubules then modify filtrate through reabsorption and secretion. From collecting ducts, urine passes via papillary ducts into a minor calyx, then a major calyx, then the renal pelvis, and then the ureter.

3B-045.text:
Simple explanation: The glomerular barrier filters by size and charge.
Why it works: Fenestrated capillaries, the basement membrane, and podocyte slits block large molecules; small solutes pass through with water.
Common mistake: Concluding that glucose in urine means it wasn't filtered; glucose is always filtered and normally reabsorbed.

3B-046.text:
Simple explanation: Three processes set what ends up in urine.
Why it works: Filtration moves plasma into the tubule; reabsorption returns substances to blood; secretion adds substances from blood to the tubule.

3B-047.text:
Simple explanation: Secretion clears substances beyond what filtration removes.
Why it works: Transporters in tubule cells move solutes into the lumen, which helps control pH and K⁺ and removes foreign compounds quickly.

3B-048.text:
Simple explanation: Reabsorption transporters can be saturated.
Why it works: Glucose filtration rises with plasma glucose, but the number of transporters is fixed; above threshold, the extra spills into urine.
Common mistake: Blaming the glomerulus; filtration is normal, and the limit is tubular reabsorption.

3B-049.text:
Simple explanation: Salt is pumped out where water can't follow, then water leaves where it can.
Why it works: The descending limb loses water to the salty interstitium, concentrating its fluid; the ascending limb removes salt from that concentrated fluid. Repeated along the loop, this builds the gradient the collecting duct uses to concentrate urine.

3B-050.text: ADH (vasopressin) promotes aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells, permitting water reabsorption down the medullary osmotic gradient. Dehydration generally triggers ADH secretion. Central diabetes insipidus involves inadequate ADH secretion; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus involves impaired renal response. Alcohol can transiently decrease ADH release, but this is not equivalent to permanent ADH deficiency.

3B-051.text:
Simple explanation: The kidney senses low pressure and starts a hormone cascade.
Why it works: Angiotensin II raises resistance right away, and aldosterone raises Na⁺ (and water) reabsorption over hours, restoring pressure.

3B-052.text:
Simple explanation: The kidneys adjust blood pH by handling H⁺ and bicarbonate.
Why it works: Each H⁺ secreted lets the tubule cell return a new HCO₃⁻ to blood, rebuilding the bicarbonate buffer.

3B-053.text:
Simple explanation: Urination needs both sphincters to relax.
Why it works: Parasympathetic signals contract the bladder (detrusor) and relax the internal sphincter; voluntary relaxation of the external sphincter allows voiding.

3B-054.text:
Simple explanation: Capillaries filter slightly more fluid than they reabsorb.
Why it works: Lymphatic capillaries collect the leftover fluid and proteins; without them, fluid would build up in the tissues.

3B-055.text:
Simple explanation: Without drainage, filtered fluid has nowhere to go.
Why it works: Protein left in the tissue weakens the oncotic force that would normally pull fluid back into capillaries.

3B-056.text:
Simple explanation: Large fat particles travel in lymph first.
Why it works: Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries but pass easily into the more permeable lacteals.

3B-057.text:
Simple explanation: Lymph re-enters the venous blood near the heart.
Why it works: Large lymphatic ducts empty into the subclavian veins, so the returned fluid joins the systemic venous return.

3B-058.text:
Simple explanation: Lymph flows like venous blood, using external compression and valves.
Why it works: Squeezing a valved vessel can only push fluid forward, toward the ducts.

3B-059.text:
Simple explanation: Nodes are checkpoints where antigens meet lymphocytes.
Why it works: Lymph from the tissues brings antigens to nodes packed with B and T cells, so lymphocytes can find and expand against their specific targets.

3B-060.text:
Simple explanation: Lymphocytes are made and trained in primary organs and activated in secondary ones.
Why it works: The thymus selects T cells that recognize MHC but not self-antigens; secondary organs concentrate antigens for those cells to find.

3B-061.text:
Simple explanation: The spleen is the immune filter for blood.
Why it works: Narrow passages trap stiff, aged RBCs for macrophages to destroy, and lymphocytes there respond to pathogens in the blood.

8C-025.text:
Simple explanation: Formal organizations are built for goals, not relationships.
Why it works: Membership, roles, and rules are defined on purpose, and bureaucracy is their typical structure.

8C-026.text:
Simple explanation: Modern societies organize life around efficient, calculable rules.
Why it works: Bureaucracies are good at coordinating large tasks, but their rules can limit individual freedom and meaning.

8C-027.text:
Simple explanation: Fast-food organization became a model for other institutions.
Why it works: Its four principles spread because they cut costs and make results predictable.

8C-028.text:
Simple explanation: Mnemonic: E-C-P-C.
Why it works: Each dimension is a way of making work more rational and manageable.

8C-029.text:
Simple explanation: Calculability means valuing what can be counted.
Why it works: Patients per hour is easy to measure, while quality of care is harder to quantify, so it gets less weight.
Common mistake: Calling it efficiency; efficiency is about the means used, while ranking by a count is calculability.

8C-030.text:
Simple explanation: Control means reducing reliance on human discretion.
Why it works: Machines and scripts limit how much individual workers vary, making outcomes uniform.

8C-031.text:
Simple explanation: Systems designed for efficiency can defeat their own purpose.
Why it works: Rigid rules and standardization ignore individual needs, which creates new inefficiencies and dissatisfaction.

8C-032.text:
Simple explanation: Organization tends to concentrate power.
Why it works: Leaders control information, expertise, and resources, so they become entrenched and pursue their own interests.

S3-001.text:
Simple explanation: Sampling is about who gets into the study; assignment is about which group they join.
Why it works: Random selection makes the sample represent the population; random placement makes the groups comparable to each other.
Common mistake: Assuming a randomized experiment automatically generalizes; that also requires a representative sample.

S3-002.text:
Simple explanation: Randomization makes groups equivalent on average before treatment.
Why it works: If the groups differ only in the manipulated variable, that variable is the best explanation for differences in outcomes.

S3-003.text:
Simple explanation: Letting participants pick their own condition creates groups that aren't comparable.
Why it works: People who choose meditation may differ systematically from those who don't, which is a confound.

S3-004.text:
Simple explanation: Randomization protects internal, not external, validity.
Why it works: Assignment balanced the groups, but the sample came from one narrow population.

S3-005.text:
Simple explanation: Quasi-experiments resemble experiments but lack randomization.
Why it works: Without random assignment, group differences other than the variable of interest can't be ruled out.

S3-006.text: This is an observational comparison of a participant characteristic, not a randomized intervention on that characteristic. Variables associated with biological sex may include multiple physiological and social factors; sex and gender are related but distinct constructs and should not be conflated. Researchers can control measured confounders or study specific mechanisms, but a group comparison alone does not establish a single cause.

S3-007.text:
Simple explanation: Participants must understand what they are agreeing to and agree freely.
Why it works: Consent respects autonomy and is valid only if it is informed, competent, and voluntary.

S3-008.text:
Simple explanation: The IRB is an independent ethics check.
Why it works: Researchers may underestimate risks in their own studies, so outside review protects participants.

S3-009.text:
Simple explanation: These principles (from the Belmont Report) underlie most research ethics rules.
Why it works: Consent comes from respect for persons, risk–benefit review from beneficence, and fair participant selection from justice.

S3-010.text:
Simple explanation: Deception is a narrow exception, not a default.
Why it works: Debriefing restores informed understanding and lets researchers address any distress.

S3-011.text:
Simple explanation: They differ in whether identities can be traced at all.
Why it works: Anonymous surveys collect no identifiers; confidential studies keep identifiers protected.

S3-012.text:
Simple explanation: People with limited capacity or freedom to consent need extra safeguards.
Why it works: Children can't legally consent, so a guardian's permission and the child's assent together respect both protection and autonomy.

S3-013.text: Informed consent is ongoing, and participants generally have the right to stop participating. Compensation should be described transparently during consent and should not exert undue influence. Prorated or milestone-based payments for work not completed can be ethically permissible; withholding compensation already earned as a punishment for withdrawal is the specific problem in this scenario.

S3-014.text:
Simple explanation: Control groups shouldn't be denied effective care for serious conditions.
Why it works: Comparing against the current best treatment still answers the research question without needless harm (the Tuskegee study is the classic violation).

S3-015.text:
Simple explanation: Confounds make it unclear what caused the effect.
Why it works: If a third variable affects both measures, the association may be due to it rather than to the IV.

S3-016.text:
Simple explanation: Look for a factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome.
Why it works: Adjusting for smoking (or comparing only nonsmokers) would test whether the coffee association remains.

S3-017.text:
Simple explanation: Internal validity asks whether the cause is right; external validity asks how widely it applies.
Why it works: Tightly controlled lab studies often have high internal validity but lower external validity, and field studies are often the reverse.

S3-018.text:
Simple explanation: Consistency doesn't guarantee accuracy.
Why it works: A scale that always reads 5 lb heavy is reliable but not valid.

S3-019.text:
Simple explanation: Blinding removes expectations from both sides.
Why it works: If neither participants nor researchers know who got the treatment, expectations affect both groups equally.

S3-020.text:
Simple explanation: Self-report depends on honesty and memory.
Why it works: People shade answers toward what seems acceptable, especially on sensitive topics when they can be identified.

S3-021.text:
Simple explanation: Causal inference needs more than covariation.
Why it works: Each feature rules out an alternative: reverse causation (temporality), third variables (randomization or control), or chance (replication).

S4-001.text:
Simple explanation: SD summarizes variability.
Why it works: It is the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean, which puts it back in the original units.

S4-002.text:
Simple explanation: Normal distributions have predictable proportions.
Why it works: Knowing the mean and SD lets you estimate how unusual a value is.

S4-003.text:
Simple explanation: Convert the score to SDs from the mean, then use the empirical rule.
Why it works: (80 − 70)/5 = 2 SD; the upper tail beyond +2 SD is about 2.5%.
Common mistake: Answering 5%, which counts both tails.

S4-004.text:
Simple explanation: The mean shows the typical effect; the SD shows how consistent it is.
Why it works: A larger SD means a wider range of individual responses around the same average.

S4-005.text:
Simple explanation: Some statistics use every value's distance; others use only positions.
Why it works: SD squares deviations, so one far-off value inflates it, while the median and IQR depend on ranks.
Common mistake: Reporting mean ± SD for strongly skewed data; median and IQR often describe it better.

S4-006.text: Adding a constant translates every observation, so distances from the mean do not change. Multiplication by c scales signed values and the mean by c; spreads scale by the absolute magnitude |c|. A negative multiplier changes the sign of the mean but cannot produce a negative standard deviation. Example: multiplying all measurements by −2 multiplies the mean by −2 and SD by 2.

S4-007.text:
Simple explanation: SD is about the data; SEM is about the mean's precision.
Why it works: Averages of larger samples vary less from sample to sample, even when individuals vary just as much.
Common mistake: Not checking whether error bars on a graph show SD, SEM, or confidence intervals.

S4-008.text:
Simple explanation: Error bars give a rough picture, not a significance test.
Why it works: Significance depends on the mean difference relative to its standard error, which shrinks with larger samples.

S4-009.text:
Simple explanation: A CI expresses how uncertain an estimate is.
Why it works: It is centered on the sample estimate and extends about ±2 standard errors for 95% confidence.

S4-010.text:
Simple explanation: CIs are about the parameter, not individual observations.
Why it works: The interval reflects the standard error of the estimate, which is much narrower than the spread of individual values.

S4-011.text:
Simple explanation: Width shows precision; narrower means a more precise estimate.
Why it works: Width depends on the standard error (SD/√n) and the critical value for the chosen confidence level.

S4-012.text: The interval for drug minus placebo is entirely negative, indicating shorter average recovery in the drug arm. A 95% confidence interval is produced by a method that captures the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under model assumptions; it is not a 95% probability assigned to the parameter. Excluding 0 corresponds to significance at α = 0.05 for an equivalent two-sided test. Causality additionally depends on study design, conduct, confounding, and assumptions.

S4-013.text:
Simple explanation: A CI that includes 0 is inconclusive, not proof of no effect.
Why it works: Failing to reject the null isn't the same as showing the null is true; a larger study could narrow the interval.
Common mistake: Concluding the treatment 'doesn't work.'

S4-014.text:
Simple explanation: For ratios, the 'no effect' value is 1, not 0.
Why it works: Relative risks and odds ratios compare by division, so equal risk gives 1.

S4-015.text:
Simple explanation: Small p-values mean the data would be surprising if there were no effect.
Why it works: Researchers set α in advance as their accepted chance of a false positive (Type I error).

S4-016.text:
Simple explanation: Statistical significance isn't the same as importance.
Why it works: Very large samples make tiny effects detectable, so look at effect size and the confidence interval.

S4-017.text:
Simple explanation: Random error scatters values; systematic error shifts them.
Why it works: Averaging cancels scatter but keeps a consistent offset, which needs calibration or a design change.
Common mistake: Confusing precision (agreement among repeated measurements) with accuracy (closeness to the true value).

S4-018.text:
Simple explanation: r gives the direction and strength of a linear association only.
Why it works: Without manipulating sleep and randomly assigning people, other explanations can't be ruled out.
Common mistake: Reading r = 0.6 as '60% of GPA is explained by sleep'; r² = 0.36 is the variance shared.

1B-040.text: Splice-site recognition is needed to remove introns accurately. A mutation at a splice junction can produce abnormal mRNA; whether a frameshift occurs depends on the number of nucleotides retained or skipped.

1C-023.text: For Aa × Aa, offspring genotypes occur in a 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa ratio. Each pregnancy is an independent event, assuming Mendelian inheritance.

2B-031.text: Transformation is uptake of extracellular DNA. Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell transfer, whereas transduction involves bacteriophages.

This Lineweaver–Burk plot shows an enzyme with and without an inhibitor. What type of inhibition is it?

Competitive inhibition. The lines share the same y-intercept (1/V<sub>max</sub>), so V<sub>max</sub> is unchanged; the inhibited line’s x-intercept (−1/K<sub>m</sub>) is closer to zero, so apparent K<sub>m</sub> increases.
This Lineweaver–Burk plot shows an enzyme with and without an inhibitor. What type of inhibition is it?

Noncompetitive inhibition. The lines share the same x-intercept (−1/K<sub>m</sub>), so K<sub>m</sub> is unchanged; the inhibited line’s higher y-intercept (1/V<sub>max</sub>) means V<sub>max</sub> decreases.

On this phase diagram (water), what does point X represent?

The triple point: the one temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium. (For water the solid–liquid line slopes slightly backward, because ice is less dense than liquid water.)
Two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which mode of inheritance does this pedigree indicate?

Autosomal recessive. Both parents must be carriers (heterozygous). It can’t be dominant, because neither parent is affected, and it can’t be X-linked recessive, because an affected daughter would need an affected father.

Which mode of inheritance best fits this pedigree?

X-linked recessive. Only males are affected, and the trait passes from an affected grandfather through his unaffected daughter (a carrier) to one of her sons. Fathers don’t pass X-linked traits to sons.
